_meta.description: Educational findings catalog for lsstack. Detection stays in Python; this file supplies what/why/prompt templates. Structure inspired by DMTF Redfish Message Registries (Platform PCIe* messages); GPU link fields crosswalked to NVIDIA DCGM PCIE LINK/MAX gen+width; SMART seed paraphrased from Scrutiny-style attribute metadata. No learn/fix URL field.

pcie.gen_mismatch.title: GPU PCIe generation exceeds platform root
pcie.gen_mismatch.what: The card’s rated PCIe generation is higher than this CPU root can run ({spec_gen_label} card on {root_max_gen_label} root; link now {cur_gen_label} x{cur_width}).
pcie.gen_mismatch.why: A PCIe link trains to the oldest generation both ends support. The CPU root’s max gen is a hard ceiling; a newer GPU cannot raise it. When the datasheet rating exceeds the platform, that is often by design, not a bad cable. Idle ASPM can still drop the displayed gen further (recheck under load).
pcie.gen_mismatch.prompt: I'm building a GPU workstation. My GPU is rated {spec_gen_label}{spec_bus_suffix}, the CPU PCIe root maxes at {root_max_gen_label}, and the link is trained at {cur_gen_label} x{cur_width}{cur_gt_suffix}. Explain what bandwidth I should expect, what I cannot fix without new hardware, and what BIOS/slot checks are still worth doing. Note idle ASPM can drop the displayed gen further.

pcie.trained_low.title: PCIe link trained below path ceiling
pcie.trained_low.what: This device path can do {path_ceiling_gen_label}, but the link is trained at {cur_gen_label} x{cur_width}.
pcie.trained_low.why: Negotiated speed is below what this path allows. On idle Linux desktops, ASPM and power management often drop the link to Gen1; treat that as a false positive until you recheck under load. Other causes: BIOS PCIe gen cap, riser/cable, or a weak slot.
pcie.trained_low.prompt: My PCIe device can do {path_ceiling_gen_label} on this path but is trained at {cur_gen_label} x{cur_width}{cur_gt_suffix}. For a home/lab workstation, what should I check (ASPM, BIOS PCIe gen, riser/cable, idle vs load), and how do I confirm the link improved?

pcie.width_limited.title: PCIe link width below CPU root max
pcie.width_limited.what: GPU width is x{cur_width} while this CPU root reports max x{root_max_w}.
pcie.width_limited.why: Fewer lanes than the root advertises. On a DIY board this is often bifurcation, a physically x8-wired “x16” slot, or lanes shared with NVMe/chipset—not a bad GPU. Confirm against the motherboard manual before replacing parts.
pcie.width_limited.prompt: My GPU is at x{cur_width} but the CPU PCIe root reports max x{root_max_w}. Explain bifurcation, shared lanes, and motherboard slot wiring in plain language, and what to look up in my board manual.

pcie.gpu_headroom.title: GPU attached with unused root lane headroom
pcie.gpu_headroom.what: CPU root has x{remaining} unused of x{max_w} while a GPU is linked at x{cur_w}.
pcie.gpu_headroom.why: Unused root width with a GPU present usually means the slot is wired narrower, bifurcation took lanes, or the card trained to fewer lanes than the root advertises. Matters most for multi-GPU peer traffic and large host↔device copies; light inference may not care.
pcie.gpu_headroom.prompt: My GPU is running at x{cur_w} on a CPU PCIe root that supports x{max_w} ({max_gen_label} max, currently {cur_gen_label}). Explain why a GPU might not use full x16 (bifurcation, slot wiring, chipset), what to check in the motherboard manual, and whether this usually matters for my workload.

pcie.oversub.title: CPU PCIe root lane oversubscription
pcie.oversub.what: Direct cards on this root need about x{consumed_width} lanes but the root max is x{max_w}.
pcie.oversub.why: PCIe lanes on one CPU root are a fixed pool. Plugging more width than the root has forces sharing or degraded links. Move cards to another root or a switch-backed slot, or reduce bifurcation consumers.
pcie.oversub.prompt: On my workstation, devices on one CPU PCIe root need about x{consumed_width} lanes but the root only has x{max_w}. Explain PCIe lane oversubscription and practical ways to rebalance slots or reduce sharing for a home/lab build.
sources: lab-builder educational (cross-check DCGM width sum vs platform design)

pcie.root_gen_low.title: CPU root trained below its max generation
pcie.root_gen_low.what: Root {bdf} supports {max_gen_label} but is trained at {cur_gen_label}.
pcie.root_gen_low.why: Child device capability, BIOS gen lock, or power saving (including idle ASPM) can hold the root link down. Recheck after a load that exercises the attached GPU or NVMe.
pcie.root_gen_low.prompt: A CPU PCIe root on my Linux box supports {max_gen_label} but is trained at {cur_gen_label}. What BIOS and software settings (PCIe generation, ASPM) should a home-lab builder try, and how do I verify the link came up higher?

pcie.link_ok.title: PCIe endpoint link looks consistent
pcie.link_ok.what: Link width and generation look consistent with this CPU root’s capability.
pcie.link_ok.why: No speed/width mismatch on this endpoint. A healthy link can still limit bandwidth if the platform gen is older than the GPU datasheet; that shows up as gen_mismatch elsewhere.
pcie.link_ok.prompt: Briefly explain how to read PCIe link status (width, GT/s, generation) on a Linux workstation and when a healthy link can still limit GPU bandwidth.
sources: DCGM link gen/width field pair (healthy baseline)

pcie.root_ok.title: CPU root lane use looks consistent
pcie.root_ok.what: Root {bdf}: x{cur_w}/{max_w} at {cur_gen_label} — lane use looks consistent with this port.
pcie.root_ok.why: Available vs in-use vs remaining is the lane budget a builder should read before adding a second GPU or NVMe on the same root.
pcie.root_ok.prompt: Explain what a CPU PCIe root port is, how lane budget works for GPUs and NVMe, and how a builder should read available vs in-use vs remaining lanes.

power.psu_undersized.title: PSU below design budget
power.psu_undersized.what: Configured PSU capacity is below the design load for this build ({budget_line}).
power.psu_undersized.why: This is design headroom, not a live PSU failure alarm. Lab inventory is the shared truth for rated watts; do not chase telemetry alone when the spreadsheet already says the brick is short.
power.psu_undersized.prompt: My lab inventory says PSU {psu_watts} W but the design budget for this GPU workstation is {budget_line}. Explain how to size a PSU for a home/college GPU lab (peak vs continuous, 12V rail, GPU spikes) and what to change in inventory vs hardware.

power.psu_unknown.title: No lab PSU capacity on file
power.psu_unknown.what: Design power budget has no PSU wattage from lab inventory for this host.
power.psu_unknown.why: Without a declared PSU, headroom cannot be judged. Enroll the system with lslab so lspower can compare estimated load to capacity.
power.psu_unknown.prompt: I'm using lsstack on a GPU lab host with no PSU watts in lab_inventory.json. Explain what fields to record for a shared lab inventory and how lspower uses them for a design budget.

disk.smart_reallocated.title: SMART reallocated sectors rising
disk.smart_reallocated.what: Drive reports reallocated (or pending) sectors above a quiet baseline.
disk.smart_reallocated.why: Reallocated sector count means the drive remapped sectors after read/write trouble. Rising counts are a wear/failure signal; a single static remap on an old drive is less urgent than growth over days.
disk.smart_reallocated.prompt: My Linux workstation SMART data shows reallocated or pending sectors on a lab drive. Explain what that means for a home/college builder, when to back up and replace, and which lsstack/smartctl fields to watch next.
sources: Scrutiny SMART attribute metadata (MIT; educational paraphrase)
